questions.q: What does a Sentinel bookmark actually save?
options: The query, the matching row or rows, and a timestamp, as a standing record
Only the name of the analyst who ran the query
A full copy of the entire Log Analytics workspace
The severity level of the current incident
questions.explain: A bookmark captures a specific query result so it can be returned to later, instead of relying on memory or a separate notes app.

questions.q: What does pinning a bookmark to an incident accomplish?
options: It attaches the saved result directly to the incident, so it shows up with its alerts, entities, and graph
It automatically closes the incident with a True Positive verdict
It deletes the original query that produced the bookmark
It raises the incident's severity to High
questions.explain: Pinning means the next analyst who opens the incident sees the bookmarked evidence as part of the incident itself, not in a separate list.

questions.q: How do pinned bookmarks function over the course of a longer investigation?
options: They accumulate into a running, timestamped case file of the evidence behind the final verdict
Only the single most recent bookmark is ever kept
They are automatically removed once an analyst logs off
They replace the need for an investigation graph entirely
questions.explain: As an analyst runs more queries and bookmarks the results that matter, those pinned bookmarks build into a case file attached to the incident.

questions.q: Why does an accumulated case file of pinned bookmarks matter for an incident's closing verdict?
options: It lets another analyst or an auditor actually verify the evidence behind a True Positive, False Positive, or Benign Positive verdict later
It is required before an incident can be assigned to an analyst
It automatically generates a new analytics rule
It replaces the investigation graph for that incident
questions.explain: The accumulated evidence makes the closing verdict something that can be checked later, instead of just taking the closing analyst's word for it.

questions.q: How do this chapter's four pieces — the queue, the graph, hunting queries, and bookmarks — relate to each other?
options: They are one connected investigation workflow in sequence, not four separate, unrelated tools
They are four competing features and an analyst only ever uses one per incident
Bookmarks replace the need for the incident queue entirely
Hunting queries can only be used after an incident is already closed
questions.explain: An incident surfaces in the queue, its graph and timelines scope what's connected, a hunting query can surface what alerts missed, and bookmarks capture the evidence — one real investigation viewed in sequence.
